public_rationale: Part of the claim holds. In November 2024, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI's next large pretrained model (Orion) lacked the big improvement GPT-4 had shown over its predecessor (e1). That fits his claim for scaling up pretrained models. But in September 2024 OpenAI reported that o1 jumped from 12% to 74% on the AIME math exam compared with GPT-4o, with large gains on other reasoning tests too (e2). On those measures, recent gains were not smaller than the GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 jump (e3). Whether 'current gains are smaller' depends on which models and which measures count, and he named neither.
limitations: The Orion evidence is a news report based on unnamed sources.
Benchmark saturation makes comparisons across eras unreliable.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Current gains in generative AI are smaller than the rapid gains of 2020-2022.

statement.excerpt: My whole point about diminishing returns is that current gains are smaller than those initial gains.

from_speaker: current gains are smaller than those initial gains
Never did any of us say there no gains at all
our_interpretation: Plain reading: the capability jumps between frontier model generations in 2023-2024 were smaller than the jumps of the 2020-2022 era, which he links to the GPT-3 to GPT-4 progression (GPT-4 training finished in 2022).
He names no measure. I use the size of benchmark and exam gains between successive frontier models, plus credible contemporaneous reporting on generation-to-generation gains.
The target period covers both sides of the comparison: 2020 through the post date.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence that recent frontier model generations (2023-2024) gave clearly smaller capability jumps than the GPT-3 to GPT-4 era, across the main measures.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that recent frontier models (2023-2024) made jumps as large as or larger than the 2020-2022 era on major capability measures.

evidence.excerpt: The model is said to be lacking the significant improvements over existing systems when compared to the gains GPT-4 made versus its predecessor.
evidence.explanation: Reports that OpenAI's next large pretrained model gave a smaller jump than GPT-4 did over its predecessor. This supports the claim for the scaling-up of pretrained models.

evidence.excerpt: On the 2024 AIME exams, GPT‑4o only solved on average 12% (1.8/15) of problems. o1 averaged 74% (11.1/15) with a single sample per problem
evidence.explanation: A 2024 model jumped from 12% to 74% on a hard math exam. That is a gain at least as large as earlier jumps on some measures, which cuts against the claim that all current gains are smaller.

evidence.excerpt: it passes a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers; in contrast, GPT‑3.5’s score was around the bottom 10%.
evidence.explanation: Shows how large the earlier GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 jump was. This is the baseline for his comparison.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: An agreed cross-era capability measure, such as Epoch-style compute-normalized benchmark trends, that shows whether 2023-2024 gains per generation were smaller than 2020-2022 gains.
